extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and other Office personnel (and patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making and documenting obviousness determinations under 35 U.S.C. 103 (including pre-AIA variants), describing the factual inquiries, permissible rationales, search scope, burden of proof, applicant reply and rebuttal evaluation. Intended to direct patent examiners in formulating proper rejections and articulating reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The obviousness inquiry is a question of law based on underlying factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere: (A) determine the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertain the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolve the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must resolve these factual inquiries and use them as the controlling inquiries in any obviousness analysis; sequence may be reordered case-by-case. Evaluate objective evidence/secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others, unexpected results) and weigh them on a case-by-case basis; presence of such evidence does not automatically decide the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulation of factual findings and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rejection must include factual findings about the state of the art and the teachings of the references, and a reasoned explanation supporting why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections cannot be mere conclusory statements; must articulate reasoning with a rational underpinning (citing KSR and In re Kahn). 35 U.S.C. 132 requires notifying the applicant of reasons for rejection so applicant can respond. Factual findings should support the rationale relied upon. Failure to follow guidelines is not appealable, but substantive rejections are appealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation of claims consistent with the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining the scope of claimed invention for the prior art inquiry, give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the specification including the claims to understand what the applicant invented (see Phillips v. AWH and MPEP §2111). The scope of the claimed invention so determined guides what to search and what references to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching/suggestion to combine, preferred searches should look for references that provide such teachings or suggestions if they exist (see MPEP §904.02). Search both explicit claim scope and disclosed but not-yet-claimed features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search / analogous art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art for 35 U.S.C. 103 may be in the applicant’s field of endeavor or in fields reasonably pertinent to the particular problem (analogous art); prior art from other fields may be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow general search guidelines (MPEP §904 to §904.03). Do not confine search to only references solving the same problem; consider references that would be reasonably pertinent even if from different fields (KSR guidance). See MPEP §§901–901.06(d) and §2121–§2129 for prior art definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indication of level of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obviousness rejection should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of the level of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding as to level of ordinary skill may be used as a partial basis for the obviousness resolution. If the only facts regarding skill are in the prior art of record, a separate specificity of skill may not be necessary (Chore-Time, Okajima). However, where appropriate, articulating the level helps maintain objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider when resolving the level of ordinary skill include: (1) type of problems encountered in the art; (2) prior art solutions to those problems; (3) rapidity with which innovations are made; (4) sophistication of the technology; and (5) educational level of active workers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every factor will be present in every case; one or more may predominate. Examiners may rely on their technical expertise to describe the knowledge and skills of a person of ordinary skill (courts have recognized examiners as persons of scientific competence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense and examiner expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel can rely on common sense and general knowledge in the art as part of the prior art, but use of common sense must be supported by evidence and a reasoned explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR permits recourse to common sense but cautions against mere conclusory assertions; when common sense is invoked to supply a missing limitation, the rationale must be searching and supported by evidence (see DyStar, Arendi). Examiners are presumed to have expertise to interpret references and to be familiar with the level of skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) rationale is valid but not rigidly required
rubrics_metrics.description: If TSM (teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine references) applies, an obviousness rejection based on TSM should be made; however, KSR cautions against overly rigid or formalistic application of TSM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSM is one valid rationale among others and may be applied where appropriate. The Office should prefer searching for references that provide TSM if they exist, but lack of an explicit TSM in the record does not bar a reasoned obviousness finding when other rationales or common sense support the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary rationales to support obviousness (list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplary, non-exclusive rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include: (A) combining prior art elements by known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) use of a known technique to improve similar devices; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement; (E) 'obvious to try' selecting among finite, predictable options with reasonable expectation of success; (F) known work in one field prompting predictable variations in same/different fields; (G) some teaching/suggestion/motivation in prior art to modify/combine references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list is illustrative, not exhaustive. MPEP §2143 and §2144 provide examples and further guidance. The key is clear articulation of why the claimed invention would have been obvious using one or more rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Obvious to try' standard and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'obvious to try' rationale may support obviousness where a finite number of identified, predictable solutions exist and there is a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR recognizes 'obvious to try' in appropriate circumstances, but caution is needed: mere experimentation or a broad field of options does not satisfy this rationale. The Office should identify predictability and reasonable expectation of success when invoking 'obvious to try'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of all claim limitations and whole-invention view
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining differences between the claimed invention and the prior art requires interpreting claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not focus only on isolated limitations; the comparison must account for the claim as a whole. Ensure proper claim interpretation per MPEP §2111 before comparing to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections must be clear in Office actions and allow effective applicant response
rubrics_metrics.description: Office actions should clearly set forth findings of fact and the rationale(s) to support an obviousness rejection so applicants can decide how to proceed and respond effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit articulation of facts and reasoning leads to prompt resolution. If factual findings are disputed, applicants must traverse with reasoned statements; examiners may repeat rejections and make actions final following MPEP §706.07(a) if traverses are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply requirements under 37 C.F.R. 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective traverse of factual findings must include a reasoned explanation why Office erred. Mere statements that a prima facie case is not established or that reliance on common knowledge lacks documentary evidence are substantively inadequate. Examiners may rely on MPEP §706.07(a) to handle inadequate traverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant’s rebuttal evidence (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence when reevaluating obviousness, including objective evidence (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others) and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After rebuttal evidence is presented, reconsider the initial determination in view of the entire record (see In re Piasecki; In re Eli Lilly). Review all rejections and proposed rejections to confirm viability. Follow MPEP §2145 and §716–§716.10 for affidavits/declarations under 37 C.F.R. 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of rebuttal evidence that can show nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuttal evidence may demonstrate that: (A) a person of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods due to technical difficulties; (B) the elements in combination do more than perform their separate functions; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such evidence is timely presented, examiners should reconsider and articulate whether initial findings remain viable. Unexpected results or technical difficulty in combining elements can overcome a prima facie case of obviousness if persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art available under 35 U.S.C. 102 is available under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103; admitted prior art can also be relied upon for anticipation and obviousness determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Panduit, Riverwood and other cited cases. Admissions in the specification or prosecution history may be used as prior art for obviousness even if they would not otherwise qualify under statutory categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain objectivity in resolving level of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving the level of ordinary skill is necessary to maintain objectivity; the determination should reflect what would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill at the relevant time, not to the inventor, judge, layman, or geniuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tailoring obviousness analysis to parties other than the hypothetical person of ordinary skill. Use relevant factual indicia and prior art to ground the determination (Ryko, Environmental Designs).
